title: ‘Guardians of the Video Game’ Lands Finecut for International Sales Ahead of Toronto Market
description: Seoul-based sales agent Finecut has acquired international sales rights to “Guardians of the Video Game,” a 3D animated feature based on the Naver W
body:
Seoul-based sales agent Finecut has acquired international sales rights to “Guardians of the Video Game,” a 3D animated feature based on the Naver Webtoon of the same name, ahead of the Toronto market.

	“Guardians of the Video Game” originated as a Naver Webtoon by Gasfard that has amassed 345 million views. The property was later turned into a mobile game on Google Play before reaching the screen as a full 3D animated feature.


	The film imagines a colorful, family-friendly realm concealed just under the surface of video games themselves, populated by a covert guild of guardians tasked with keeping each title operating and preserving every player’s journey. Its central figure, a guardian banished from sleek 3D gaming worlds, tumbles into an obscure, pixel-based RPG. There, working in secret, he steers an unsuspecting hero toward the game’s conclusion while working to expose a plot targeting both him and the game itself.
	

	Uhm Young-sik directs the feature, adding to a filmography that includes the animated film “Running Man: Revengers” and the animation portion of “Yumi’s Cells” Season 1. He earlier co-directed “Red Shoes and the Seven Dwarfs,” a title that reached distribution in 120 countries.

	Animation and VFX studio Locus Animation produces “Guardians of the Video Game.” The company’s credits include “Red Shoes and the Seven Dwarfs” and “Exorcism Chronicles: The Beginning,” the latter of which now has a sequel in production. Locus Animation has built a broader slate around adaptations of popular webtoons, among them “Barkhan” and “Denma.”

	“Guardians of the Video Game” is currently in post-production and slated for release in the fourth quarter of 2026. Its first footage will be revealed through Finecut during the Toronto market. 
	

	Finecut brings several other titles to Toronto this year. “Long Long Night,” a 3D animated feature, will hold its Toronto premiere in the festival’s Centrepiece section. “Nowhere to Lay My Eyes,” from director Hong Sangsoo, picked up two Pardo Awards at Locarno this year – one for best direction, another for best performance – along with the festival’s Ecumenical Jury Prize.

	Also on the slate is “Dora,” directed by July Jung and starring Kim Do-yeon and Ando Sakura, an invitee to Cannes’ Directors’ Fortnight. Park Hoon-jung’s noir “Tristes Tropiques” rounds out the lineup; the film won the Silver Raven Award from Brussels International Fantastic Film Festival and picked up invitations from Sitges, Fantasia, Fantasy Filmfest and L’Étrange Festival.

schema.headline: ‘Guardians of the Video Game’ Lands Finecut for International Sales Ahead of Toronto Market

title: Duane ‘Keffe D’ Davis Found Guilty of Orchestrating Tupac Shakur’s Murder
description:
A jury has found Duane “Keffe D” Davis guilty of orchestrating the 1996 murder of Tupac Shakur.

	After a day of closing arguments, Davis was found
body:
A jury has found Duane “Keffe D” Davis guilty of orchestrating the 1996 murder of Tupac Shakur.

	After a day of closing arguments, Davis was found guilty of murder with the use of a deadly weapon with the intent to promote, further or assist a criminal gang, according to ABC News. Davis, 63, faces a maximum of life in prison.

	The jury deliberated for roughly three hours after a weeks-long trial in Las Vegas. Prosecutors and police claimed that Davis orchestrated Shakur’s murder in a drive-by shooting in Las Vegas on September 7, 1996, and handed the gunman the murder weapon. They believe that the actual shooter was either Orlando “Baby Lane” Anderson, Davis’ nephew, or another man who was in the backseat of a car.
	

	During his closing arguments, prosecutor Binu Palal said that the case was “drenched in circumstantial evidence” and corroborating witnesses, in addition to Davis’ own statements over the years to media and in his own memoir to show that he was guilty of aiding the murder. “For nearly 18 years, Duane Davis has told the police, television, books, YouTube interviewers — anybody that will listen, he has told — he is responsible for the murder of Tupac Shakur,” said Palal. “Tell him you hear him — find him guilty.”

	Davis’ attorney Michael Sanft, meanwhile, argued that the only proof that Davis was responsible for Shakur’s murder was through his own confessions, which did not constitute real evidence.

	“We have to ask ourselves the question really at this particular point: Why are we here 30 years later if Duane Davis had actually confessed — truly confessed?” he said.
	

	Davis is scheduled to be sentenced on October 13 and will be held without bail. He shared that he plans to appeal the sentence once it’s handed down.

	On the night of Sept. 7, 1996, Shakur was shot four times with a Glock .22 pistol while his car was stopped at a red light in Paradise, Nev. The bullets came from a white Cadillac that had pulled up alongside Shakur’s vehicle — which was being driven by his label boss, Marion “Suge” Knight — and struck the hip-hop artist in the chest, arm and thigh, while one of the bullets grazed Knight in the head. Shakur succumbed to his injuries six days later.

	Shakur’s murder has long been one of music’s most notorious unsolved crimes. Over the years, Davis boasted about his purported role in Shakur’s killing. In 2018, to drum up anticipation for his upcoming memoir, he appeared in the BET docuseries “Death Row Chronicles,” where he discussed the night of Shakur’s murder, suggesting that the murder weapon was passed from someone in the backseat of the white Cadillac, but he wouldn’t say who. “Going to keep it for the code of the streets,” Davis remarked, adding, “It just came from the backseat, bro.”

	Davis released his memoir, “Compton Street Legend,” in 2019, whose intro stated, “I’m one of the only living eyewitnesses to Tupac’s killing,” before describing the night of Shakur’s killing in detail. In the book, Davis claims that he got a Glock and entered the white Cadillac with three others, looking for payback against Shakur and Knight for what they’d done to Anderson. “No words exchanged, the time for talking had passed, the shit was about to go down!” he wrote.

	Prosecutors brought the case against Davis in September 2023, claiming he orchestrated the murder after Shakur’s entourage attacked his nephew just hours before Shakur’s death at age 25.

schema.headline: Duane ‘Keffe D’ Davis Found Guilty of Orchestrating Tupac Shakur’s Murder

title: The Rise of ‘Love Island USA’: From Death Threats Against Contestants to Agency Battles for the Biggest Stars
description: When Liv Walker first heard from the “Love Island USA” casting team, she thought it might be a scam. After all, she had never even seen the show.
body:
When Liv Walker first heard from the “Love Island USA” casting team, she thought it might be a scam. After all, she had never even seen the show.

	Originally scouted for Season 5 of the reality dating show, Walker turned down the initial offer. But when the casting team reached out again for the sixth season a year later in 2024, she decided to give the show a shot.

	That decision changed her life. 

	Season 6 went on to transform the U.S. installment of “Love Island,” distinguishing itself from the U.K. version that had popularized the idea of dropping a group of young, ready-to-mingle strangers together into a private villa cut off from the outside world.

	“Love Island USA” originally aired on CBS when the show launched in 2019, with comedian Arielle Vandenberg hosting. The series switched to Peacock for its fourth season, replacing Vandenberg with Sarah Hyland — before Ariana Madix officially took over as host in Season 6. Following her dramatic break-up with Tom Sandoval, the “Vanderpump Rules” star brought the Bravo audience over to Peacock, and the dynamic cast kept them watching. 

	“When I first got kicked off the show, I remember one of the talent managers was like, ‘Hi! Just a head’s up, the show did better than ‘Bridgerton,’” Walker tells Variety. “I was like, ‘What do you mean, better?’”


	Season 6 of “Love Island USA,” which is produced by ITV America and airs on Peacock every summer, saw its viewership double compared to that of previous seasons, according to NBCUniversal. Those numbers have only continued to grow in the two years since. This past summer, Season 8 drew 19 billion minutes watched, translating to 7.9 million views, according to data from Peacock.

	The newly Bravo-fied “Aftersun” spinoff, now co-hosted by “Summer House” star Ciara Miller, saw a 135% increase in viewership from last season. And with other spinoff series such as “Beyond the Villa” and “Love Island Games,” many Islanders continue their journey far beyond their original seasons.


	For Walker, Season 6 was the beginning of what she calls “the catapult.” For the franchise, it was the beginning of a transformation from a reality dating series into something much larger — one that would transform its contestants into global celebrities and content creators in the process.


	“I don’t think we’ve seen anything quite like this,” says UTA unscripted TV agent Jamie Youngentob. “The closest thing would probably be Bravo, but those shows can take multiple seasons for somebody to really break through and stick.”



	

					Season 6: Daniela Noelle Ortiz-Rivera, Leah Kateb, Kaylor Martin 
									Courtesy of Ben Symons/Peacock
	



	The Season That Changed Everything
	

	Season 6 had taken the world by storm, but its success wasn’t the result of contestants entering the villa with dreams of becoming influencers. In fact, several of the season’s Islanders say the opposite was true: They had no idea anyone would be watching at the scale they ultimately were.

	Kaylor Martin, who appeared alongside Walker in Season 6, was a senior in college when she applied. She was working three jobs, had about 4,000 Instagram followers and rarely posted on social media. 

	“I don’t think any of us had expectations on our lives being changed,” Martin tells Variety, noting that she and her fellow Islanders had plans to return to work or school after the show. 
	

	That naivete, she believes, is part of what made Season 6 resonate. The cast wasn’t performing for an audience they knew was watching.

	“If I wasn’t on Season 6, and I was asked to go on Season 7 or 8, I don’t know if I would have cried that much or acted so organically because we truly had no idea everyone was watching,” Martin says.

	The result was a group of contestants whose lives changed almost overnight. Martin went from being a college student to, two years after leaving the villa, working as a full-time content creator and host of the podcast, “Kaylor’s Crash Out Podcast.” 

	Nobody expected Season 6’s spike in popularity, including creatives and talent agencies. When Martin left the villa, she didn’t prioritize brand deals or posting consistently because she didn’t realize social media could become a career. 

	She says “Love Island” now helps its contestants navigate the transition, connecting Islanders with agencies and publicists after they leave the show — something Season 6 didn’t offer. After having to navigate that process largely on her own, Martin is now eager to help Islanders from recent seasons with their post-villa journey. Most recently, she connected with Season 8 contestant Kenzie Annis and gave her advice on growing her platform. 

	Now, leading talent agencies view “Love Island” as a viable pipeline for creators looking to build long-term careers. It has become an increasingly competitive space to scoop up talent, says UTA partner and agent Mahzad Babayan, with the agency signing Season 8 winner Bryce Alakai just over a week after the finale aired. Gersh, meanwhile, reps Emmy-nominated host Madix and Season 8 contestant Annis.

	But for agents working in the digital creator space, it’s not about securing the buzziest “Love Island” Islanders with the biggest brand deals — it’s about finding the right talent who are looking for longevity over a viral moment, far past the one-year exclusivity deal that limits what opportunities “Love Island” contestants can take. That usually means keeping them in the NBCUniversal family.

	“The talent know, now more than ever, what they’re getting into,” says Gersh’s head of digital Jade Sherman. “‘Love Island’ is an incredible brand, and they try really hard to protect their IP. They’ve put things in place to do that, and it’s on us as representatives to be able to pivot and adapt to where their changing rules are.”

	For UTA, signing Alakai was attractive because he already had a “real” career in music before going on the show, and even appeared in a Tubi film. 

	“He’s been working incredibly hard at pursuing and building a DJ career,” Youngentob says. “That was exciting for us, alongside our music colleagues.”
	

	The Islanders who followed in Seasons 7 and 8 entered a franchise that was already a proven launching pad to worldwide fame and opportunity.

	Amaya, who won Season 7, was working as a registered nurse when a casting producer reached out to her. Like Walker, she had never watched a full season of “Love Island,” and her exposure to the show primarily stemming from viral clips on social media. 

	Unlike the Season 6 cast, though, Amaya entered the villa knowing what the previous season had become. But the show’s newfound fame didn’t sway her decision to apply.

	“I feel like life is all about taking risk,” she tells Variety about deciding to join the show. “You just have to trust your intuition, and it was the best thing I did.”

	After becoming a fan favorite of Season 7 and being crowned its winner, Amaya was determined to pursue other opportunities beyond reality television. She’s now working on music, exploring her passion for poetry and taking acting classes, all opportunities that launched from her time on the show. 

	“Thank God I decided to take the chance and to take the risk and to not let self-doubt hold me back,” she says. “That’s just the message that I’m trying to give overall — ‘Why not?’” 

	Starring alongside Amaya in Season 7 was Iris Kendall, who was originally scouted for Season 6 but declined. When she decided to accept the offer for the seventh season, the success of the previous season made her anxious about stepping into the public eye. 

	“Honestly, in a perfect world, if it wasn’t filmed and I did the social experiment, that would be freaking awesome,” Kendall tells Variety, laughing. “But it definitely made me nervous to be in the public eye and have people critique every single thing that I could possibly do, especially when the cameras are on you 24/7.”
	

	By the time Kendall left the villa, the scale of the franchise had grown even larger. At the Season 7 finale, the cast was told the season had performed seven times better than the previous one.

	And the opportunities followed. Kendall signed with WME and turned what she expected might be a handful of brand deals into a full-time career.

	“I just thought I’m going to get maybe some deals here and there, but I didn’t think that I was going to be doing anything that I’m doing now or having this as a full time career,” she says about her success after the show. “I’m just so thankful that I put myself out there to the public.”



	

									Courtesy of Peacock
	



	Fame Has a Price

	But underneath the brand deals and business ventures lies an increasingly attached fanbase analyzing the Islanders’ every move. After getting her phone back and seeing the world’s reaction to Season 7, Kendall says she quickly learned that fans could develop strong opinions about Islanders based solely on what they’ve seen on television and social media. 

	“We have parasocial people commenting on our lives,” Kendall says. “They don’t really know us. They don’t know what we text about. They don’t know what we talk about.”

	While the Islanders are in the villa, they’re completely oblivious to the fact that an entirely new universe forms on social media among those tuned into the show. Viewers take it upon themselves to determine who the token heroes and villains of the season are, often fighting over just how well a contestant should be liked. 

	In Season 7, fans notably targeted contestant Huda Mustafa, turning her vulnerable moments into widespread memes (yes, we’re talking about her “dream date”). In Season 6, fans honed in on Andrea Carmona, quickly labeling her as an antagonist.

	“I was not expecting that. I had to get off of social media for two weeks,” Carmona tells Variety. “My TikTok for you page was just people saying very nasty things about me, and this whole narrative that I knew in my heart wasn’t me. But at the end of the day, people are going to perceive you however they want.”

	The feeling that viewers personally know the people they’re watching on screen could stem in part from the fact that the show is on six days a week each summer, which gives audiences hours upon hours of consistent access to the Islanders’ lives.
	

	“Younger fans are drawn to it as appointment-viewing television, because a lot of what is transpiring on screen are relationship dynamics that they might identify with themselves, so there is a lot of projection onto the cast of characters. And that creates an entirely new show,” says Brandy Monk-Payton, assistant professor at Fordham University. “It’s almost as if there is the show that exists on Peacock, and the show that exists on TikTok.” 

	Danielle J. Lindemann, the author of “What Reality TV Says About Us,” adds, “There’s this whole other discourse happening online that you almost have to follow in order to watch and understand the show. You kind of have to do them both in tandem.”

	Additionally, viewers engage with “Love Island” on a much higher, more intense level than other reality dating shows because they’re able to directly vote on which couples they want to stay together and, ultimately, which couple takes home $100,000 on finale night.

	“Who you enjoy, who you want to win, becomes a projection of your identity and so you have all of these conflicts online that are just proxy wars,” Bonk-Payton adds.

	Carmona says that, even two years after her season, she still gets hate messages from those still parasocially attached to Season 6. 

	“I generally say from my season, I’m happy that I was the one that got all this hate because truthfully, I don’t think anyone on that season could have handled the amount that I got and still be here today. That’s how bad it was.”

	Daniella Bondar, an admin of a “Love Island” Facebook group with more than 300,000 members, says that people get reported every day for hateful comments, although she notes that the group remains mostly positive and cordial. Discourse in the group continues long after the show airs, with members keeping up with the contestants from past seasons via social media and clamoring for details about their lives.

	“When I watched the show, I didn’t know what the problems with Zach were, but then I go to the group and I see the big discussion is that everybody thinks he’s here just to be on social media, just to be famous, they didn’t like him,” Bondar says. “They’re taking all the things they see on TikTok and Instagram and then bringing it back into the group to see how everybody else feels.”

	False narratives and misconceptions are common in “Love Island,” largely stemming from the fact that Peacock creatives are tasked with condensing 24 hours of footage into one-hour episodes. That sometimes means key elements of a contestant’s personalities, their relationship dynamics and their friendships don’t make it into the final cut. 
	

	“What matters the most to me is how the people in my life view me, how I treat other people, and if I’m doing a good job at that,” Kendall says about receiving negativity from viewers with false perceptions of her. “That’s what’s important to me, not what random people say or what random people think.”

	To help control the negative comments online and bullying online, Peacock released a statement ahead of Season 8 prior to the first episode airing, reminding fans to “keep it kind” and “keep it positive.” A similar statement was released in Season 7, reminding fans that the Islanders are “real people.” 



	

					Season 7
									Courtesy of Jocelyn Prescod/Peacock
	



	Building Community

	With the Season 8 reunion dropping on Aug. 31, the Islanders — who have strategically been quieter on social media than contestants from past seasons, and have done limited press in the lead-up to the reunion — are ready to move into the next phase of their lives outside the “Love Island” bubble.

	Unlike Walker, who might as well have appeared on an entirely different show than what the Season 5 Islanders experienced, contestants who get off the show now know they have a community of past “Love Island” Islanders to connect with. 

	That’s an especially important point for Carmona, who extends a hand to contestants facing hate.

	“We all trauma bond together,” Carmona says. “No one understands the experience of what we went through.”

schema.headline: The Rise of ‘Love Island USA’: From Death Threats Against Contestants to Agency Battles for the Biggest Stars

title: ‘Gargoyles’ Live-Action Series Not Moving Forward at Disney+
description:
The live-action “Gargoyles” reboot has turned to stone.

	The project, which was in early development at Disney+, is no longer moving forward, a sou
body:
The live-action “Gargoyles” reboot has turned to stone.

	The project, which was in early development at Disney+, is no longer moving forward, a source confirms to Variety.

	It was announced in 2023 that the streamer was working with writer Gary Dauberman and James Wan’s Atomic Monster to develop a live-action version of the beloved Disney animated series, which aired from 1994 to 1997.


	Rumors that the reboot was not moving forward originated from an interview by ComicsOnline with Greg Weisman, co-creator of the original series. “That’s dead,” Weisman said when asked about the Disney+ project. “I have no idea about animation, but there are no current plans for live-action.” Weisman was not directly involved in the live-action reboot, but a source close to the project confirmed its status to Variety.
	

	Dauberman (“It”) would have served as writer and executive producer of “Gargoyles” 2.0 with Wan also executive producing. Disney Branded Television was attached as the studio. The logline for the project read: “Based on the cult classic Disney animated series, Goliath is the last of a heroic race of gargoyle warriors who once lived among mankind. Free from a centuries long curse that turned him into stone, Goliath struggles to solve the mystery of his past while watching over modern-day New York City alongside police detective Elisa Maza.”

	The original “Gargoyles” hailed from Walt Disney Television Animation and was considered dark for the Mouse House. The show followed a fantastical species known as gargoyles, who are made of stone during the day but come alive at night. When a clan of gargoyles living in Scotland in the late 10th century are betrayed and cursed by a magic spell, they cannot break from their stone sleep until a thousand years later in modern New York, thanks to the intervention of a wealthy industrialist named David Xanatos. The gargoyles decide to claim New York as their new home and vow to protect it.
	

	The voice cast of the show included Keith David, Salli Richardson, Jonathan Frakes, Marina Sirtis, Ed Asner, Thom Adcox-Hernandez, Jeff Bennett and Bill Fagerbakke. It aired for three seasons in the 1990s, with the final season retitled “Gargoyles: The Goliath Chronicles.”

	“Gargoyles” had a strong cult following, and there have been various rumors and attempts to bring the series back to life over the years. None have ever come to fruition.

schema.headline: ‘Gargoyles’ Live-Action Series Not Moving Forward at Disney+

title: AMC Theatres Launches Indie Distribution Label Leawood Films; Veteran Hollywood Execs to Advise
description:
AMC Theatres is entering the indie film fray.

	The world’s largest movie theater chain announced Monday it will launch Leawood Films, a distributio
body:
AMC Theatres is entering the indie film fray.

	The world’s largest movie theater chain announced Monday it will launch Leawood Films, a distribution venture advised by a trio of veteran Hollywood executives — including former Warner Bros. Motion Picture Group chairman Toby Emmerich, Apple and Disney marketing whiz Ricky Strauss and former Paramount distro head Kyle Davies.

	Leawood will “focus solely on films fully financed by their filmmakers, or already completed films, leveraging AMC’s exhibition, marketing, and distribution expertise to expand the supply of movies for a broad array of movie theater operators across the U.S. and internationally,” the announcement said. Emmerich and Strauss will consult, while Davies will help pilot the label as a full-time employee.
	

	The move means that Davies is leaving his post as president of distribution at Bleecker Street.


	Leawood is named for AMC’s Kansas headquarters, and its inception comes as the domestic box office is enjoying an undeniable revival (“Obsession,” “They Odyssey” and “Spider-Man: Brand New Day” are just a few of the titles packing in audiences this year to levels not seen since pre-COVID times).

	The theater chain will have some key questions to answer about Leawood in the coming days. As an acquirer of films either financed or finished, it’s safe to say that representatives from Leawood will attend the annual film festival circuit in search of product. That would put them squarely in competition with the studios and fellow indie labels looking for titles, though the Leawood announcement said prominently that the company is “designed to be additive and not expected to compete with AMC’s longstanding studio and distribution relationships.” It’s also unclear if AMC will provide Leawood with its own marketing budget to attract moviegoers.
	

	“Leawood Films is being created with a straightforward objective, given that substantial excess capacity exists in the movie theater industry: to bring more movies to theaters,” said AMC Theatres CEO Adam Aron. “If we can take steps to ensure that a few extra movies come to theaters each year, it is gravy for AMC in the United States and Odeon in Europe, as well as for our fellow exhibitors.”

	Emmerich, Strauss and Davies will report to Aron. The company is repped by Craig Jacobson, a leading entertainment attorney and a founding partner of Hansen Jacobson. 

	AMC has gone it alone on distribution in the past, notably for the juggernaut concert films “Taylor Swift: The Eras Tour” and Beyoncé’s “Renaissance.”

schema.headline: AMC Theatres Launches Indie Distribution Label Leawood Films; Veteran Hollywood Execs to Advise

title: Writer and Comedian Marty Nadler Dies at 80
description: Marty Nadler, a producer, sitcom writer and stand-up comedian, who worked on “Happy Days,” “Laverne and Shirley” and “The Odd Couple,” died in Marga
body:
Marty Nadler, a producer, sitcom writer and stand-up comedian, who worked on “Happy Days,” “Laverne and Shirley” and “The Odd Couple,” died in Margate, Florida, on Aug. 26. He was 80. His son, Charlie Nadler, said he died due to complications from myasthenia gravis.

	Born in the Bronx in 1945, Nadler eventually switched coasts to pursue a career in comedy. He discovered his passion for stand-up as a theater major at Ithaca College. He established a close personal and professional relationship with director Gary Marshall, and contributed jokes to nine of Marshall’s movies, including “Pretty Woman,” “Runaway Bride” and “Mother’s Day.” Marshall considered Nadler his good luck charm, and gave him on-screen cameo roles in each of those movies. 
	

	In 1976 when Nadler was writing for “Laverne and Shirley,” he met a new writer named Holly Mascott who met with him at Paramount to pitch story ideas. She eventually became Nadler’s wife. They married on Martha’s Vineyard in 1978, and bought a home there in 1984, where their only child, Charlie, was born.


	Nadler’s son followed in his footsteps, and they performed stand-up together around the country. They recently recorded their act at The Garry Marshall Theatre in Los Angeles titled “A Boomer and A Millennial Walk Into a Special.” It will be released in early 2027 by Comedy Dynamics. “It was a magical evening with family, friends, and colleagues from all chapters of dad’s life in attendance,” Charlie Nadler said.  

	Nadler is survived by his ex-wife, with whom he remained close friends; their son Charlie and daughter-in-law Cary Kandel. Nadler will be interred on Martha’s Vineyard.

schema.headline: Writer and Comedian Marty Nadler Dies at 80

title: Gal Gadot Defends Starring in Movie With AI Sets and Lighting Because ‘You’re Going to Work With It or Be Out of the Game’; Lawyers Spent 6 Months Ensuring AI Would Not Alter Actors
description: Gal Gadot appeared on the “Happy Sad Confused” podcast to promote her Prime Video action movie “The Runner” and told host Josh Horowitz that she wou
body:
Gal Gadot appeared on the “Happy Sad Confused” podcast to promote her Prime Video action movie “The Runner” and told host Josh Horowitz that she would likely not return as Wonder Woman if an opportunity to make a third movie came to be.

	“For me to go to do another Wonder Woman, I am not sure I would at this point in my life with four children and different schools and all of that,” Gadot said. “To check out from all of them for such a long period of time, it doesn’t work for my life anymore at this point.”
	

	Gadot played Wonder Woman in Zack Snyder’s DC Universe, debuting in 2016’s “Batman v Superman: Dawn of Justice” before headlining 2017’s “Wonder Woman.” The standalone movie, directed by Patty Jenkins, was a blockbuster hit with $824 million at the worldwide box office. Gadot would appear in “Justice League” the same year before reuniting with Jenkins for 2020’s “Wonder Woman 1984.” 


	Jenkins was developing an idea for “Wonder Woman 3” when James Gunn and Peter Safran took over DC Studios, effectively ending Snyder’s tenure. While Gadot had claimed in 2023 that a third “Wonder Woman” would be developed in the rebooted DC Universe, sources told Variety at the time Gunn and Safran would not be moving forward with another Gadot-led sequel. The actor was ultimately not surprised when she got the boot. 

	“I saw the way everybody else was handled. The Henry [Cavill] situation was not handled elegantly to say the least. Patty [Jenkins] was not handled elegantly. We’re all adults and we’re all good,” Gadot said on the “Happy Sad Confused” podcast about the transfer of DC Studios power. “I am so grateful I got the opportunity to wear these boots and have the character be so celebrated. I can only wish whoever is next comes pure to this journey. This character means so much to so many of us. It was never mine. I was always just a vessel. This is Hollywood.”
	

	Gadot also spoke about her upcoming role in Doug Liman’s “Bitcoin,” which has garnered controversy for using AI to create the movie’s sets and lighting. The cast, which includes Gadot opposite Casey Affleck, Pete Davidson, and Isla Fisher, was shot in a completely barebones space. The film’s producer, Ryan Kavanaugh, has claimed the $70 million production saved more than $200 million by using AI to fill in the production design and lighting.

	“This was the longest contract I have ever worked on,” Gadot said of the movie. “It was six months from my lawyers to go through every scenario we could think about as far as the AI component of it. I did not want AI to have anything to do with my performance. We had to protect that, to such an extent that SAG called my lawyers to ask for pointers to update the SAG contract to protect other actors. As far as the performances, it’s all me.”

	Gadot continued, “I am afraid of AI, but I am going to be afraid and look away? No. I am afraid but I am playing with it and learning it and trying to educate myself. The train has left the station. You’re going to work with it or be out of the game completely. I am trying to make the best of it and protect what I can protect. The AI component in this movie is for sets and the lighting. We had a broad crew and a lot of people were working on this movie.”

	Because Liman shot all of the actors in what amounts to a barebones warehouse, Gadot compared the experience to working in theater because it was essentially only the actors on set.

	“It felt like a pure art form of creating a movie,” she explained. “I haven’t seen a single shot. As an actress, I wait so much. There’s the legendary quote: ‘You are being paid to wait as an actor.’ Here we would film nonstop because we didn’t have to wait for lighting. We would film on and on and on for 10 hours. It was amazing… as actors you’re always hot. You don’t cool off. We’ll see. It’s crazy.”

	Watch Gadot’s full interview on the “Happy Sad Confused” podcast in the video below.

title: Trump Endorses U.S. Tax Incentive to Keep Hollywood Production: ‘Let’s Get This Done!’
description:

body:
President Trump on Monday endorsed a federal tax incentive for film and TV production, a move long sought by Hollywood studios and unions.

	In a statement posted to Truth Social, Trump said he will push for a bipartisan bill to save the industry.

	“I am going to suggest that Republicans and Democrats get together, and immediately craft Legislation to save the Movie, Television, and Entertainment Business in America,” he wrote. “Congress should approve, immediately, a Federal Production Incentive to create Entertainment Jobs in America. It can be done quickly, accurately, efficiently and, importantly, will benefit ALL of America. What we watch on the Silver Screen should be made in what was once the Movie and Motion Picture Capital of the World. Let’s get this done!”
	

	Since last year, Trump had repeatedly threatened to impose a 100% tariff on films made overseas. Industry stakeholders have sought to redirect his attention toward a tax credit, much like those offered by Canada, the U.K., and by 39 U.S. states.


	Several Democratic lawmakers have gotten behind the idea, notably including Sen. Adam Schiff, who held a hearing on the topic in March. But Schiff and others have said that Republican lawmakers were waiting on a positive signal from the White House getting on board.

	Charles Rivkin, the CEO of the Motion Picture Association, applauded Trump’s move in a statement.

	“For over a century, American studios, casts, and crews have produced the films and series that the world wants to see,” Rivkin said. “A federal incentive would be a landmark step toward bringing more production to local communities in all 50 states, strengthening our nation’s economy, and making our country a more competitive place to produce, create, and tell great stories. We applaud President Trump’s support for this vital action, and we look forward to continuing to work with the White House and bipartisan leaders in Congress to enact a meaningful and effective national incentive into law.”
	

	Supporters of the measure have cited a dramatic drop in domestic production since the streaming bubble burst in 2022. Around 73,000 jobs have been lost nationwide, about two-thirds of them in Los Angeles.

	Schiff circulated draft legislation last year that would have provided a 15% credit on labor costs incurred in the U.S. The MPA has been working with Jon Voight, Trump’s “special ambassador” to Hollywood, to push for a 20% credit.

	In his Truth Social post, Trump said he had recently met with Voight on the issue.

	“He is a fantastic man who loves our Country, and feels strongly about the Motion Picture and Television Industry,” Trump wrote. “He hates what’s happened to it! It is being dissipated in its entirety. It has moved to Canada, and other Countries, with very little work being done anymore in the United States. Hollywood is a Complete and Total Disaster! Despite the name, it is getting very little work. There is no incentive to be there, and it is hurting California very badly.”

	Trump argued that a federal incentive would generate a positive return on investment.

	“Jon, and many others in the Industry, are suggesting we do Federal Tax Incentives in order to Make our Movie and Television Production Business GREAT AGAIN, perhaps GREATER THAN EVER BEFORE!” he wrote. “The amount of money spent on Tax Incentives will be made up tenfold by the money pouring into the Treasury’s coffers.”

	Some lawmakers have also been working to revive Section 181, a much more modest tax code provision that allowed independent producers to accelerate depreciation of film investments. That provision expired last year.

	A federal tax incentive, by contrast, would give studios and producers a credit or a rebate on a percentage of production costs. That credit would likely stack on top of state-level credits offered in California, New York, Georgia, New Jersey, and other states. Some 80 countries have adopted tax incentives as an economic development tool, and production centers have flourished in Central and Eastern Europe, Australia, South Africa, and other parts of the globe.

	Supporters of a federal incentive have argued that it would benefit states that currently do not see much production, such as Florida and Michigan, because they do not offer state-level incentives.
	

	Schiff, who led Trump’s first impeachment in 2019, also applauded the announcement in a statement on X.

	“I am in strong agreement with the President,” he said. “Congress should immediately take up and pass a federal film tax incentive to bring back these good-paying jobs that we’ve lost to other countries. Let’s work together — Republicans and Democrats — to get this done, and bring the movie magic back to America.”

	Rep. Laura Friedman, a Democrat from Burbank, has also been working with Republicans in the House on  an incentive for the past year.

	“I agree that our tax incentive legislation needs to pass – and to pass quickly,” she said. “For more than a year I’ve been sitting down with Jon Voight, Congressional colleagues, the unions, studios, and producers to build the case for a national film and television tax credit. There’s no reason Canada, the UK, or Australia should be taking our jobs. We still have the best crews on the planet. It’s time we made it possible for them to stay where they belong: in America.”

	The Directors Guild of America has also been pushing for a federal incentive, and got the studios to commit to lobbying for it during negotiations in June.

	“We look forward to working with the Administration and Congress on a bipartisan bill that will have the greatest possible impact on promoting domestic film and television production, creating good jobs, and strengthening America’s homegrown film and television industry,” said Russell Hollander, the union’s national executive director.

title: ‘Sacred Creatures’ Review: Slippery Canadian-Italian Satire Follows the Cult and Collapse of a Questionable Guru
description: As the great Aretha Franklin taught us, it’s usually a backhanded approach to begin a critique with praise for the gowns. Or gown, in the case of “S
body:
As the great Aretha Franklin taught us, it’s usually a backhanded approach to begin a critique with praise for the gowns. Or gown, in the case of “Sacred Creatures,” a microbudget hothouse drama otherwise not given to ostentatious styling. Still, it’s a pretty defining dress. Worn for the bulk of the running time by enigmatic focal character Miriam (Olivia Luccardi), it’s both shapeless and striking, equal parts haute couture showstopper and military parachute, while even its color is hard to pin down: regal gold in some lights, bilious chartreuse in others. In a tall tale of a fey outsider elevated to cult-leader status by a passionate mob, costume designer Francesca Cibischino is to be commended on creating a garment that captures both the otherworldly godliness that others see in its wearer, and the girlish absurdity that we do.
	

	In its peculiar changeability and clownish grandeur, the gown could also be a metaphor for Canadian writer-director Frieda Luk‘s intriguing, elusive debut feature — which itself never quite settles on a style or form, roving itchily between barbed social satire, mythic holy-fool fable and dysfunctional family drama. There is potential in all these modes, but for all the compelling ideas thrown into “Sacred Creatures,” most viewers won’t be altogether sure what to take away from it. Luk’s darkly airy tone, however, is genuinely, compellingly unusual, and should be an asset to future works with a slightly sturdier dramatic foundation. Following a premiere in the main competition at Edinburgh, the film could pick up limited international distribution on the strength of its Euro-American cast and overall curiosity factor.
	

	The setting is semi-rural northern Italy, pretty far in all senses from the Tuscan sun: No tourist would linger long in this flat patchwork of farmland, light industry and retail parks, under seemingly perennially overcast ecru skies. The impressive, rambling country house in which the film is largely set really demands more glamorous surroundings, but its owner, middle-aged Italian artist Renzo (Antonio De Matteo), tries valiantly to make it a bohemian enclave, filling it with stark modern sculpture and hard-partying friends; his younger Canadian partner, Ray (James Cusati-Moyer), struggles to feel at home.

	That air of discontent is ramped up when Ray’s two sisters descend on the house for a brittle family reunion. Toronto career woman Michelle (Romina d’Ugo) arrives bearing an assortment of anxieties and resentments; at least some of those relate to Miriam, the baby of the family, who recently spent some time in a mental health facility following an episode that her family would describe as a psychotic breakdown, and Miriam as a spiritual breakthrough. Though evidently fragile, Miriam projects a kind of beatific, benevolent calm, and it’s to the credit of Luccardi’s canny performance that it’s ambiguous whether she knows something that everyone else does not, or simply nothing at all. 

	Either way, it’s a magnetic quality: Renzo’s aspirational aunt (Pia Engelberth) is entranced by her at a party — where Miriam first dons the head-turning gown — and soon rustles up a coterie of local admirers to gather and fawn over the exotic, spectacularly dressed newcomer. When the dazed young woman reels off quotes from an obscure self-help book, her new acolytes take her words as gnomic wisdom. Her new following grows by the day, as Luk’s script drily observes just how little it takes to become an influencer, even outside the online sphere. 

	“Sacred Creatures” starts to lose its satirical footing, however, as Miriam becomes a veritable cult leader and even a religious icon, the scope of proceedings expanding so fast and so far that credibility is strained past breaking point. The sibling drama, meanwhile, rather fades out of view amid these loftier goings-on; the film’s narrative begins to feel devised by the old parlor game Consequences, repeatedly wrenched in erratic new directions. It holds your attention, though, as does the filmmaking, with its muted, desaturated canvas with key, unsettling stylistic flourishes: DP Nicolas Villegas’ queasy deployment of shallow focus, disorientingly muffled sound design at certain junctures, and of course that dress, ostensibly bound to a character, but floating through this world like an unknowable spirit.

title: Michael Strahan Looks Back at How America Healed After 9/11 With ABC News’ ‘United We Stand’ Special
description: Michael Strahan was a little more than halfway through his NFL career when 9/11 happened. The defensive end spent all 15 seasons of his pro football
body:
Michael Strahan was a little more than halfway through his NFL career when 9/11 happened. The defensive end spent all 15 seasons of his pro football career with the New York Giants.

	One ominous moment from that catastrophic period that Strahan will never forget took place on the Giants’ practice field outside MetLife Stadium in East Rutherford, N.J. The World Trade Center’s twin towers, just across the Hudson River in lower Manhattan, were easily spotted from the stadium. Until they weren’t.
	

	But the sudden change in the skyline wasn’t the only haunting sign of what had been lost.


	“I remember seeing cars – a parking lot full of cars for people who were never coming back to claim those cars,” Strahan recalls of the area around the stadium. “It was something that just smacked you in the face.”

	As the 25th anniversary of the terrorist attacks on the World Trade Center and the Pentagon, Strahan was motivated by his memories to pursue a different kind of 9/11 retrospective special, ABC News’ “9/11: United We Stand – 25 Years Later.” The two-hour program, set to air on ABC, Disney+ and Hulu on Sept. 1, explores how sports, music, comedy and the arts helped the country move forward after the unimaginable loss of nearly 3,000 victims and the blow to the armor of American invincibility that the meticulously planned attack represented.

	For a change, Strahan and his producing partner Constance Schwartz-Morini and others sought to put the emphasis on the joyful, inspirational, galvanizing and cathartic moments that the nation experienced in the days after the attacks. There were personalities and moments that consoled a grieving country.
	

	A quarter century later, Strahan is no longer sacking quarterbacks. After retiring from football following the 2007 season, he made a successful segue into sportscasting on “Fox NFL Sunday” in 2008. He joined Kelly Ripa as co-host of “Live With Kelly and Michael” from 2012 to 2016. Since 2016, he’s been an anchor for ABC’s “Good Morning America.” 

	RELATED STORY: Disney Plans Hours of 9/11 Coverage Across ABC, Disney+ and Nat Geo 

	As Strahan thought about the significance of the 25-year milestone for 9/11, he found himself remembering the feeling of unity and national pride that emerged amid the shock that a terrorist plot to hijack commercial aircraft could kill thousands of people, destroy the World Trade Center and severely damage the Pentagon.

	“Everybody handled it in their own way, and everybody got through it in their own way. But there were some catalysts for people who felt very hopeless at the time — being in sports, entertainment, music and Broadway,” Strahan says. “I wanted to have everybody tell their story, but yet honor those who suffered. You’ll go from joy to happiness and laughter and sadness. You just feel everything. But it’s a good reminder of where we were, where we’ve come and hopefully where we hope to get back to.”

	Notables who take part in the special include Derek Jeter, Jon Bon Jovi, Matthew Broderick, Billy Crystal, Pete Davidson, Jimmy Fallon, Mark Messier, Jon Stewart as well as Strahan’s ABC News colleagues Robin Roberts, George Stephanopoulos, and Martha Raddatz. It was produced by SMAC Productions, A+E Factual Studios, Derek Jeter’s Cap 2 Productions and The Montag Group for ABC News Studios,

	For Strahan, being part of one of New York’s highest-profile sports teams at a time when the city felt under siege was a profound experience that taught him about the deeper meaning of sports. At first, he wondered how any team would return to a normal NFL schedule after the horror that struck just two days after the start of regular-season NFL play that year. But as the enormity of the loss sank in, Strahan realized that sports and teams that people love would play a huge role in moving the country forward.

	“I learned that when you have people who hurt in one area of this country, everybody can feel that hurt. And when you feel that hurt as an American, other Americans step up and really want to be a part of the healing process,” Strahan recalls. 
	

	The Giants were on the road for their first few games that season. The team was blown away by the response from Kansas City Chiefs fans when they played in Arrowhead Stadium just 12 days after the attacks.

	“They were passing around firemen helmets and police caps to the fans in the stands. They raised hundreds of thousands of dollars that the team matched to just show their love and support — not just for New York City but for the country as a whole. We all had to heal,” Strahan says. “Within these 25 years there has been a lot of healing, but there’s still a long way to go.”

	Strahan says the process of looking back at the recovery from the shock to the American system made for sharp contrast to the bitter red state vs. blue state political polarization that has permeated the country in recent years. The sense of solidarity and resolve that Americans demonstrated in the months after 9/11 was powerful.

	“I think it is something that is very important for us to remember and to remember the feeling we had. That is what I feel was lost, and I think hopefully in this film, people will see where we were and say, “OK, that’s the feeling I want. That’s the love I want. That’s the way I want this country to feel.’ And maybe we can get back to that,” Strahan says.

	The special highlights key moments for the country in the wake of the attacks, from concerts that Jon Bon Jovi and Paul McCartney hosted for first responders to the triumphant return of Broadway shows including “The Producers” after the Rialto resumed performances on Sept. 13.

	One of the most poignant parts of the special is a candid interview with Pete Davidson. Davidson’s father, Scott Matthew Davidson, was a New York City firefighter who died on 9/11 when his son was 7 years old. Davidson has declined past offers to take part in 9/11 remembrance specials and events. Strahan’s ties to New York and reputation as a broadcaster made Davidson say yes this time.

	“To have Pete in it really meant the world because you can see still a lot of emotion for him tied behind it, but at the same time, you watch this guy have the ability to take that pain and make you laugh at times when you’re going through something,” Strahan says. “His way of getting through all that pain has been through comedy, which I think has led to him having a career that he’s had.”
	

	ABC News has hosted a few screenings of the special in New York in advance of its premiere on ABC, Disney+ and Hulu. Strahan has been gratified by the response.

	“So many people came up at the screening and said, ‘This is something that everyone at school should see.’ Kids should see this because it lets you know how serious it was, but yet how resilient and how amazing we are as Americans to get through all of this,” Strahan says “The humanity that we showed in that time frame, the love that we show for each other as Americans. There wasn’t such divide and I think that’s a great message for where we are right now. We all just want the same things. We want family. We want love. We want safety.”

title: Duane 'Keffe D' Davis Found Guilty In The Murder of Tupac Shakur
description:
Keffe D
                          Found Guilty in Tupac Murder
body:
Keffe D
                          Found Guilty in Tupac Murder
                      
                  
                                                                        Published 
                              August 31, 2026
                            5:22 PM PDT
                                                                            
      
    
        
                    
                  
      
    
            A Las Vegas jury has found Duane "Keffe D" Davis guilty of murder in the first degree in the death of Tupac Shakur.
      
    
            The jury returned its verdict Monday, convicting Davis of murder with the use of a deadly weapon with the intent to promote, further or assist a criminal gang. The 63-year-old now faces a possible maximum sentence of life in prison ... although he has already made it clear to the judge he plans to appeal the verdict.
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            Prosecutors never claimed Davis fired the fatal shots during the September 1996 drive by shooting. Instead, they argued he was the "shot caller" who handed the murder weapon to the gunman, believed to have been his nephew, Orlando "Baby Lane" Anderson, or another man riding in the back seat.
      

            The verdict marks the first conviction in connection with Tupac's murder, one of the most notorious unsolved killings in music history.
      
    
            Prosecutors never accused Keffe D of pulling the trigger himself. Instead, they argued he orchestrated the Las Vegas shooting as retaliation after Tupac and his entourage got into a fight with Keffe D's nephew earlier that night.
      
    
            They pointed jurors to Keffe D's own police interviews and his memoir, including a 2008 interview in which he told investigators he handed his nephew a gun and said his nephew was the one who fired the fatal shots.
      
    
            His attorney, meanwhile, argued Keffe D's admissions were nothing more than tall tales, telling jurors his client was "full of crap" and that's why he was never charged for decades.Over the course of the trial, jurors heard testimony from two dozen prosecution witnesses and just three defense witnesses. Keffe D did not testify in his own defense.
      
    
            The guilty verdict marks the first conviction in connection with Tupac's murder.

title: See Hayden Panettiere's Boyfriend Brian Hickerson Hiding Under Table Before 2025 Arrest
description:

body:
Hayden Panettiere's Boyfriend
                          Wild Photo Shows Him Hiding Under Table Before L.A. Arrest
                      
                  
                                                                        Published 
                              
                August 31, 2026
                
                            4:41 PM PDT
                                                                      |
                                                                Updated 
                                  August 31, 2026
                                6:56 PM PDT
                                    
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            Hayden Panettiere's boyfriend Brian Hickerson was seen barefoot and hunkered down under a restaurant table moments before his 2025 Los Angeles arrest ... and TMZ has obtained a photo from the bizarre scene.
      
    
            The pic was snapped August 2, 2025 inside Barney's Beanery in West Hollywood ... showing Brian sitting on the floor underneath a table with his shoes off as a Los Angeles County Sheriff's deputy stands nearby.
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            Sources with direct knowledge tell TMZ ... Brian came into Barney's and appeared to be under the influence of something and acted erratically. Sources say he allegedly broke a drinking glass at the bar. We're told things escalated when Brian allegedly threw one of his shoes at another person who was eating inside the restaurant ... prompting staff to ask him to leave.
      

            Our sources say Brian started freaking out and an employee attempted to physically remove him ... but he refused to go, so cops were called. We're told law enforcement also had a difficult time getting Brian out of the restaurant ... but deputies eventually removed him and arrested him outside.
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            The owner of Barney's Beanery tells TMZ ... Brian was not permanently banned from the restaurant. He's allowed to return.
      
    
            Prosecutors declined to file charges due to insufficient evidence. He was arrested again four days later for allegedly being under the influence of a controlled substance, entered a diversion program and had the case dismissed after completing 10 Narcotics Anonymous meetings.
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            TMZ also broke the story ... Brian was permanently banned from at least three South Carolina bars two to three months before Hayden's death, with sources telling us those bans stemmed from concerns over excessive drinking.
      
    
            As you know, Brian was with Hayden August 16th when she was found unresponsive. He used Narcan in an attempt to revive her, to no avail. Her death is currently under investigation.
